compression.title: PennSound
compression.lede: is an ongoing project of the University of Pennsylvania's Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing, producing new audio recordings of poets and preserving existing audio archives, free to stream and download; the archive reads it as a witness that credits author, performer and co-composer as separate attributions.

sentences.text: PennSound is an ongoing project committed to producing new audio recordings and preserving existing audio archives: a poetry website and online archive that hosts free, downloadable recordings of poets reading their own work, and of others' work.

Its own YouTube channel calls it a Web-based archive for noncommercial distribution of the largest collection of poetry sound files on the Internet, and its Instagram account the world's preeminent online archive of poetry audio, with more than 50,000 recordings from 1913 to the present.
It has been called the "iTunes for poetry", a phrase Wikipedia attributes to Charles Bernstein in an Associated Press article, and its running series of posts is PennSound Daily.

It is a project of the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing at the University of Pennsylvania, whose site lists it among the Center's programs beside the Kelly Writers House events and ModPo, under the Center's director, Al Filreis; PennSound itself is directed by Charles Bernstein, Filreis and Chris Mustazza and edited by Michael S. Hennessey, with Danny Snelson and Kenneth Goldsmith as senior editors.

Two other descriptions name two directors: the description on its YouTube channel lists Bernstein and Filreis as directors, Hennessey as managing editor and Mark P. Lindsay as managing director, and a profile on poets.org, posted in December 2006, calls Bernstein one of the site's two directors along with Filreis.

Filreis and Bernstein created it, and it was launched in 2005; an article on Penn Today under the title "PennSound: All the Free Poetry You Care to Download" opens by setting it against a recording industry that "may not want anyone downloading music without paying for it".

Recordings are filed on author pages, series pages, anthology, collection and group pages and in a singles archive, with Cinema, Classics, podcast and Close Listening collections and the PennSound Daily archive beside them.

Readings are broken down into singles, one poem to a file, and complete readings are also kept; a 2006 profile set this organization against "many poetry audio archives", and newly segmented readings, cut by poem and by topic, continue to be announced.

The PennSound Manifesto, by Bernstein, sets six rules, among them that recordings be free and downloadable and broken down into singles, that all files be named, that bibliographic information be embedded in each file, and that sound files be indexed and retrievable from a library catalog under the poet's name and from search engines on the web; the About page links it and the launch press release.

The census records that a work is held under the poet's name on an author page and under a series name on series pages, such as Belladonna* and Love Jawns: A Mixtape, and that the saved pages state no policy on pseudonyms, heteronyms or collective names.

The archive's paper on heteronymy holds that a civil name is the atomic unit of attribution across the systems that govern scholarly, literary, institutional and platform production, copyright among them, and it distinguishes the pseudonym, which changes the label attached to an authorial function, from the heteronym, which changes the organization of the function itself.

Where the reader differs from the author, a recording names both: the historical selection on the home page lists John Clare's "Vowelless Letter" (1849) performed by Charles Bernstein, Hannah Weiner's Clairvoyant Journal performed by Weiner, Sharon Mattlin and Rochelle Kraut, Kurt Schwitters's "Ur Sonata: Largo" performed by Ernst Schwitters (spelled "Scwhitter" on the page), and Velimir Khlebnikov's "Incantation by Laughter", translated and performed by Bernstein.

A co-composer is credited the same way, the music and performance of one piece being by Christopher Reiner "and included with permission", and the selection itself is signed "Selected by Charles Bernstein".

The archive reads PennSound as a witness of a distinct type: a recording keeps the author's name, the performer's voice and a co-composer's credit as separate attributions, so that a reading of one poet's work by another collapses into neither, and its filing rule is the poet's name, with no evidence beyond the names it files under of whether a chosen name is kept as given.

In the archive's account of heteronymy, ordinary translation, role-playing "understood as performance rather than as sustained authorial organization" and collaborative authorship that constitutes no distinct heteronym fall outside the concept, and a heteronymic architecture is said to make a collapse of plural functions register as loss; the census, for its part, tags PennSound as not limited to the poet's own voice.

Its holdings run from historic recordings by Ezra Pound, Wallace Stevens, Guillaume Apollinaire, William Carlos Williams and H.D. to what Wikipedia groups as more recent recordings, by Allen Ginsberg, John Ashbery, Jack Spicer, Gertrude Stein and Lyn Hejinian, with readings and sometimes musical versions of classical Greek poetry, Chaucer, Milton, Pope and Shakespeare; its historical selection opens with Apollinaire's "Le Pont Mirabeau" of 1913.

A 2006 profile gave its emphasis as "the experimental and adventurous", across emerging and canonical poets, and the census gives its coverage as recordings from the 1910s onward, from the United States and elsewhere, with no geography stated.

Its size is stated in two units: Wikipedia gives over 1500 full-length and single-poem recordings, "the largest collection of poetry sound-files on the internet", and in another sentence well over 50,000 sound files, while its Instagram account gives more than 50,000 recordings; its own saved site pages state no count.

Its recordings come from the poets themselves, from universities and institutions such as Harvard University's Woodberry Poetry Room, and from poets' estates, and it states the limit of its record: "We intend to provide as much documentation about individual recordings as possible; new bibliographic information will be added over time," with supplements invited.

A 2006 profile reported the manifesto's commitment to recordings "with as much bibliographical and archival information as possible" and called the archive committed to dates and documentation for all of its recordings; the census counts complete bibliographic data for every recording among what the resource does not answer.

Its newest collection, announced on 27 March 2026, is a home for Charles Ruas's radio programming from the 1970s, 1980s and 2000s, launched with hundreds of recordings and "still under construction"; the Eric Mottram Centennial Collection is another.

The PennSound Podcasts are produced by Al Filreis at the Kelly Writers House and listed on Jacket2, where episode 84, with Gina Myers, is dated 1 April 2026 and the editor, Hennessey, presents episodes of his own; his retrospective podcast, PennSound Rewind, received its own page in March 2026 and is published at PennSound and at Jacket2.org.
With the Kelly Writers House and the Poetry Foundation it sponsors PoemTalk, a podcast discussing a different poet or poem each show.

The census records it as active, with PennSound Daily posts from November 2025 to March 2026, and the newest listing on its home page is George Quasha reading genius foci at Barrytown, New York, on 14 July 2026.

Its files are free to stream and download as MP3s and are intended for non-commercial use by anyone, teachers and libraries included; the description on its YouTube channel states the terms in full: "All PennSound recordings are made available for noncommercial and educational use only; the featured writers and artists retain all copyrights to their work."

The census, reading its site pages and its encyclopedia article, records the rights terms of individual recordings as not stated, counts who holds the rights to a recording among the questions the resource does not answer, and leaves any rights or permissions statement unchecked.

A March 2026 post on its home page counts PennSound among "publicly funded distribution platforms" and presents the kind of programming that is lost when funding to the institutions that produce it is "suddenly cut for political reasons".

It works in collaboration with the Kelly Writers House, UbuWeb, the Electronic Poetry Center, Jacket2, the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing and the University of Pennsylvania Libraries; its About page thanks UbuWeb and the Electronic Poetry Center, UbuWeb's creator Kenneth Goldsmith is among its senior editors, and the census enters UbuWeb, the Electronic Poetry Center and Jacket2 as its neighbours.

Others describe it in their own terms: poets.org in 2006 as "a free online gallery, archive and radio show rolled into one"; ModPo, the site of a course in modern and contemporary American poetry, as "the largest archive of recordings of poets reading their own poems"; and its own X account, joined in March 2009, as an "audio & video archive of poetry & poetics" associated with the Kelly Writers House.

On YouTube its channel has 2.16K subscribers and 338 videos; a one-minute video titled "Charles Bernstein - PennSound" is on The Brainwaves Video Anthology's channel, and two longer videos, of 51:52 on PennSound's channel and 54:21 on a channel named Jerry Inspired, carry no title beyond the platform's name.

The leesharks.com authorship census, which admits a resource that gathers and holds many works or records and says what it holds, enters PennSound as an empirical comparator in the areas of avant-garde and experimental archives and of attribution and credit, and asks of it how authored performance is recorded: whose voice a recording carries and under whose name it is filed, with performer and author credited apart.

The census's anchors are the archive's paper on heteronymy and its essay on the existence tax, and its organizing question asks how authorship is made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed.

By the census's account the resource answers whether a recording of a named poet is held, who performs a recording where the performer differs from the author, and which reading series and events it has recorded, and it leaves unanswered how an author who writes under several names is filed; the census leaves the author pages, series pages and singles archive themselves to later reading, and Wikipedia's article, the field's encyclopedia source, was last edited on 22 September 2026.

Asked for the name on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview, at a new address, gave PennSound as "the world's largest free digital archive of poetry audio, featuring over 50,000 recordings spanning from 1913 to the present", with its host, its directors, its singles, its scope and its programs, and the Capture Registry found the host and the three directors exact and the Ruas collection carried, the 2005 launch left out.

The registry traces the count to the Instagram card and Wikipedia's "Well over 50,000 sound files", and the year 1913 to Apollinaire's recording, and notes that the composition calls all the files recordings and names T.S. Eliot, who appears in none of the three PennSound pages the census saved.

It found the separate credits absent: the composition files everything under author pages, "individual catalogs for thousands of writers", in keeping with the manifesto's rule of the poet's name, and has no place for a reading of one poet's work by another, the feature that makes PennSound a row of the census; the registry's analysis calls the archive composed accurately at its grain.

The registry scored the composition's provenance at 0.25, the three directors and the Center named and the sources carded, and records PennSound as an external resource entered in the census on 1 November 2026 with its own pages saved by hash.

CAP-1-09.quote: 'PennSound is the world's largest free digital archive of poetry audio, featuring over 50,000 recordings spanning from 1913 to the present.' … Twelve cards: CPCW, Jacket2, Wikipedia, YouTube (four), poets.org, Penn Today, X, Instagram, ModPo.

CAP-1-04.quote: The innocent reading first. Asked for the name, the Overview says what the archive is, where it is based, who directs it, how its files are cut and what it runs.

CAP-1-01.quote: HOST AND DIRECTORS EXACT. 'Co-directed by Al Filreis, Charles Bernstein, and Chris Mustazza.' … The new Charles Ruas collection is carried … The 2005 launch is not carried.

CAP-1-06.quote: THE ARCHIVE AND ITS DIRECTORS EXACT; THE CHARLES RUAS COLLECTION OF 2026 CARRIED; ITS CREDITING OF PERFORMER APART FROM AUTHOR NOT CARRIED

CAP-1-02.quote: THE COUNT. 'over 50,000 recordings spanning from 1913 to the present' follows the Instagram card and the saved article's 'Well over 50,000 sound files', and the 1913 the home page's 'Guillaume Apollinaire, "Le Pont Mirabeau" (1913)'. … the composition calls all the files recordings. Of the four poets it names in its scope, T.S. Eliot appears in none of the three saved PennSound pages.

CAP-1-03.quote: THE CREDITS NOT CARRIED. The census row reads PennSound as a witness of a distinct type, where author, performer and co-composer are credited apart … The composition files everything under 'Author Pages: Extensive, individual catalogs for thousands of writers', matching the manifesto rule the article reports … and has no place for a reading of one poet's work by another.

CAP-1-05.quote: The archive composed accurately at its grain, with its directors and its newest collection carried. The feature that makes it a census row, a performer and a co-composer credited beside the author, is absent.

CAP-1-08.quote: The three directors and the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing named; sources carded.
